newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. scientists scour universe for advanced life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. scientists scour universe for advanced life.

text.p: As movie-goers marvel at "Contact," a film about the quest for intelligent life on other planets, a real-life search of the universe is being directed from an ordinary-looking office building in California's Silicon Valley.

It is the headquarters of the SETI (Search for ExtraTerrestrial Intelligence) Institute, a privately funded organisation that uses radio telescopes to scour the universe in the hope of finding a radio signal from another planet. "Contact," starring Jodie Foster, portrays a search similar to the SETI Institute's "Project Phoenix."

While several other groups are involved in similar quests, the institute says Project Phoenix is "the world's most sensitive and comprehensive search for extraterrestrial intelligence." It is focusing its search for radio signals on 1,000 nearby Sun-like stars, hoping that some of them have orbiting planets with advanced civilisations.

Project Phoenix scientists are looking for signals either beamed deliberately toward our solar system or emitted by another planet's television or radar. So far they have not detected any, but SETI Institute President Frank Drake is confident they will eventually. "Just don't ask me when. It may be a long, long time," he said.

The institute is enjoying a surge of public interest because of movies like "Contact" as well as Pathfinder's landing on Mars this summer and last year's revelation that a meteorite found on Earth may contain evidence of a primitive form of microscopic life on Mars billions of years ago.
"Discovering another civilisation in space is the last great adventure left for humans to do," Drake said in an interview at the SETI Institute's Mountain View offices.

The makers of "Contact" sought advice from institute scientists and the fictional account echoes real life in some areas, such as the battle to convince sceptical government officials the search is worth funding. The institute raised private funds to continue its "targeted search," which was launched by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in 1992 but cancelled by Congress a year later to save money.

As in "Contact," the director of Project Phoenix is a woman who is passionate about her work. Jill Tarter was a friend and colleague of the late astronomer Carl Sagan, on whose novel "Contact" is based, but says she was not the model for the character played by Foster in the movie.
"Carl wrote a book about a woman who does what I do. ... He didn't really write a book about me," said Tarter, 53, who calls her work "absolutely the best job in the whole world."

The oldest unanswered question posed by humans was whether they were alone in the universe, she said in a telephone interview. "We used to ask priests and philosophers. But this generation, for the first time, scientists and engineers have an opportunity to do an experiment that could answer the question on the basis of fact. I just couldn't imagine anything more important."
TWO TELESCOPES POINTED AT THE STARS

The institute is currently using two radio telescopes -- a giant telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia, with a backup at Woodbury, Georgia, to confirm findings. A sophisticated computer system at Green Bank "creates in effect a 56 million channel radio receiver," Drake said.

Special equipment automatically searches for signals that could be of intelligent extraterrestrial origin and the information is relayed back to a control room at Mountain View. The scientists have found thousands of "candidate" signals, which at first glance could have emanated from another planet, but on closer investigation all have been found to be produced by humans. Often they are signals from spacecraft or reflected from aircraft.

"A few weeks ago we had a real exciting episode where we had two signals about one megahertz in frequency apart which had all the earmarks ... of a true extraterrestrial signal. Everybody got very excited," Drake said. But the hopes were dashed when the signal turned out to come from a spacecraft.

Drake, 67, who first searched for extraterrestrial signals in 1960, says he believes the probability that intelligent life exists elsewhere in the universe is 100 percent. He ponders how people would react if scientists ever did find a signal from another planet.

"Would people be frightened? Maybe, yes. The optimists such as me think that people will be elated because it will open the window to a vast new body of knowledge, which will enrich our civilisation," said Drake, who is also an astronomy professor at the University of California at Santa Cruz.

Project Phoenix was funded by donations from technology entrepreneurs such as Hewlett-Packard Co. founders William Hewlett and the late David Packard, Intel Corp. Chairman Gordon Moore and Microsoft Corp. co-founder Paul Allen.
Funding for the $4 million-a-year project is assured through the year 2000. The institute is seeking to raise a $100 million endowment to ensure its long-term survival.
